newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Cuts, turbulence ahead for SAS - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Cuts, turbulence ahead for SAS - analysts.

text.p: Scandinavian airline SAS is expected to unveil a sweeping cost-cutting programme when it posts its nine-month results next week, but this will not remedy all the carrier's woes, analysts said on Thursday.
With competitors eager to muscle in on the lucrative Nordic routes it dominates, analysts said only huge savings would help smooth the bumpy ride ahead of the airline.
"SAS has been living in a child's nursery -- sheltered from competition in its own backyard," said a transportation analyst at a Danish bank, speaking on condition of anonymity.

"If you look at Lufthansa, they have already experienced competition for several years from Deutsche BA. KLM has no home market. British Airways has been operating in a deregulated market for 10 years with much lower prices," he said.
"SAS is in a more difficult situation than the other European airlines. I think their share could drop further."
Analysts do not expect SAS's nine-month results, due on November 19, to match the 1.01 billion crowns ($152 million) earned in the third quarter of 1995.
SAS made a full year 1995 pre-tax profit of 2.63 billion crowns ($395.9 million).

Norwegian carrier Braathens SAFE, which this month launched six daily flights between Stockholm and Oslo, said last Friday it plans to expand its frequent flyer programme to include flights on Transwede, a domestic Swedish airline it half owns. .
Aviation insiders say British Airways which signed a franchise deal with Denmark's Sun-Air in May, appears to be positioning for a major assault on SAS.
Virgin Express, British tycoon Richard Branson's short-haul airline, started cut-price daily flights from Brussels to Copenhagen in September.
One analyst said SAS had reduced prices by 14 percent on the Oslo-Stockholm route, and could lose a 25 percent market share.

"We expected a shortage of planes to limit competition this year. But what we've seen is that competition is strengthening for SAS faster than we expected. We didn't expect Braathens to come in that early. Ditto for Virgin," another analyst said.
Media reports, unconfirmed by SAS, said the airline would announce savings of one billion crowns over the next two years.
Analysts said this would still not be enough. "It will come too late and it will be too difficult to implement," one said.
One analyst said any cost-cutting measures should be seen in light of savings plans announced by rivals KLM, Swissair and British Airways.

"If SAS is going to match that, we're talking about a rate of about four to five percent a year." he said, "So if they come out and say we are going to be real tough now and cut costs by one billion crowns, that would actually be disappointing."
Strong Scandinavian unions threaten the airline's ability to cut costs -- pilot strikes lost SAS market share in Norway.
"Airlines that exist in the future will be those best at managing relationships with the unions, cutting costs while maintaining good relationships with them," an analyst said.
Danish commercial bank Den Danske Bank downgraded the airline's shares and earnings estimates, saying higher fuel costs could knock 30 percent off SAS' 9-month profits

In its November 1 report,the bank expected SAS to post a profit after depreciation for the third quarter of 1996 of 658 million crowns, down from 1.01 billion in the same 1995 period. ($1=6.643 Crown)
